question.text: Find the equation of the line containing the point $(-1,1)$ that is perpendicular to $2x-3y=-5.$
question.explanation:
First, we write the equation $2x - 3y = -5$ in its slope-intercept form, as follows: \begin{align*} 2x-3y &=-5 \\ -3y &= -2x - 5 \\ y &= \dfrac{2}{3}x + \dfrac{5}{3} \end{align*}

Since perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other, the slope of the new line should be the negative reciprocal of the slope of the given line $y=\dfrac{2}{3}x+\dfrac{5}{3}.$ The given line has a slope of $\dfrac{2}{3},$ so our perpendicular line must have a slope of $-\dfrac{3}{2}.$

Our perpendicular line must have the slope $m=-\dfrac{3}{2}$ and pass through the point $(x_1,y_1) = (-1,1).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line:

\begin{align*} y - y_1 &= m(x - x_1) \\[5pt] y - 1 &= -\dfrac{3}{2}(x - (-1)) \\[5pt] y - 1 &= -\dfrac{3}{2}(x + 1) \\[5pt] y - 1 &= -\dfrac{3}{2}x -\dfrac{3}{2} \\[5pt] y &=-\dfrac{3}{2}x -\dfrac{1}{2} \\[5pt] 2y &= -3x -1 \\[5pt] 3x +2y &=-1 \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Equation of a Line Perpendicular to a Line in Standard Form

question.text: Find the equation of the line that passes through the point $(1,-2)$ and is perpendicular to the line passing through the points $(-1,2)$ and $(4,3).$
question.explanation:
Perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other.

First, let's find the slope $m_1$ of the line passing through the points $(-1,2)$ and $(4,3)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} m_1 &= \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3-2}{4-(-1)} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4+1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{5} \end{align*}

Since we want a perpendicular line, the slope $m$ of the line we're trying to find must satisfy \[ m \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right) = -1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad m = -5. \]

We know that the line passes through the point $(1,-2).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line:

\begin{align*} y - y_1 &= m(x - x_1) \\[3pt] y - (-2) &= -5(x - 1) \\[3pt] y + 2 & = -5x + 5 \\[3pt] y &= -5x+3 \end{align*}

question.text: Find the equation of the line that passes through the point $(8,-1)$ and is perpendicular to the line passing through the points $(-4,1)$ and $(1,-3).$
question.explanation:
Perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other.

First, let's find the slope $m_1$ of the line passing through the points $(-4,1)$ and $(1,-3)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} m_1 &= \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{-3-1}{1-(-4)} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{-3-1}{1+4} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{4}{5} \end{align*}

Since we want a perpendicular line, the slope $m$ of the line we're trying to find must satisfy \[ m \cdot \left(-\dfrac{4}{5}\right) = -1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad m = \dfrac{5}{4}. \]

We know that the line passes through the point $(8,-1).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line:

\begin{align*} y - y_1 &= m(x - x_1) \\[5pt] y - (-1) &= \dfrac{5}{4}(x - 8) \\[5pt] y + 1 &= \dfrac{5}{4}x - 10\\[5pt] %y + 1 &= \dfrac{5}{4}(x-8)\\[5pt] y &= \dfrac{5}{4}x - 11 \end{align*}
